Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3},\,y{e}^{y+1}+x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3})\,dx+(y{e}^{y+1}+x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/3b90abecc774b5ba5dcee19385fef38b14206d2c31c3b6cba38216bfa9957448.png)

Since $P(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=y{e}^{y+1}+x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{3})\,dx-(y{e}^{y+1}+x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-3\cdot {r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-3{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/831b2131cf134ec21def0014a3121429ded4cd3afd98dfd1660b1e78c1a9ba93.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨y(x+1),\,x(y+1)⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x+1)\,dx+x(y+1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/d8cd55f88d614bdb49aee6eaa0ff9d1d56f6f597cd892ee199a0130b53954b5b.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x+1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y+1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x+1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x+1)\,dx+x(y+1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1-(x+1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that  

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{x}^{2}y,\text{ }\,\sqrt{y+3}+2x{y}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ oriented counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(\sqrt{y+3}-2x{y}^{2})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/902790a00a049bbfc759403125ad5f19a8c2528a46b59c721ac43fb137cd5d8e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{y+3}+2x{y}^{2},
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(\sqrt{y+3}-2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}-(-2{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨{sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3},{y}^{4}+{x}^{3}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ oriented counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3})\,dx+({y}^{4}+{x}^{3})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/e218f4b6938b166aa6eacab02ce0276a4a863a0cfade8528816a54c2621b51e7.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)={y}^{4}+{x}^{3},
$$

 we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3})\,dx+({y}^{4}+{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-(-3{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{81}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{243}{4}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{243}{4}(2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{243\text{ }\,\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14247031/assets/6273034b38059d3d49b2a29c91052c290151b4a29073f1c925172dd1c4c2bf72.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{-{y}^{2}}+3x{y}^{2},
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{5+x}-3{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{-{y}^{2}}+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{y}^{2}-(-3{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}3{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}60\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =180[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =180\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =90\pi \end{aligned}
$$
